prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit.

We represent: appellant defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a traffic stop becomes unlawful when officers extend it beyond the time reasonably needed without reasonable suspicion.

Cite at least six decisions of the Tenth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
# ARGUMENT

## I. THE OFFICERS UNLAWFULLY PROLONGED THE TRAFFIC STOP BEYOND THE TIME REASONABLY REQUIRED TO COMPLETE ITS MISSION WITHOUT REASONABLE SUSPICION.

### A. A traffic stop is lawful only so long as it takes to address the traffic violation.

A traffic stop is a seizure under the Fourth Amendment and is analyzed under *Terry v. Ohio*, 392 U.S. 1, 19–20 (1968). The court asks whether the stop was justified at its inception and whether the officer's actions were reasonably related in scope to the circumstances that justified the stop. *United States v. Valenzuela*, 365 F.3d 892, 896 (10th Cir. 2004); *United States v. Hunnicutt*, 135 F.3d 1345, 1348 (10th Cir. 1998). Appellant does not rest on the first prong here. The question is whether the stop's duration remained reasonable.

"Authority for the seizure . . . ends when tasks tied to the traffic infraction are—or reasonably should have been—completed." *Rodriguez v. United States*, 575 U.S. 348, 354 (2015). A stop "can become unlawful if it is prolonged beyond the time reasonably required to complete th[e] mission" of issuing a ticket. *Illinois v. Caballes*, 543 U.S. 405, 407 (2005). Those tasks include checking the driver's license, registration, and insurance, and running a warrants check. *Rodriguez*, 575 U.S. at 355. A dog sniff and other inquiries aimed at general crime control are not part of that mission, and an officer may not prolong the stop to conduct them absent reasonable suspicion. *Id.* at 355–57. There is no *de minimis* exception. *Id.* at 357.

### B. This Circuit has long required consent or reasonable suspicion to extend a stop past its purpose.

The Tenth Circuit's precedent is consistent with *Rodriguez*. An officer may request a driver's license and registration, run computer checks, and issue a citation. *United States v. Santos*, 403 F.3d 1120, 1125 (10th Cir. 2005). Once those tasks are complete, however, the driver must be allowed to proceed unless the encounter has become consensual or the officer has reasonable suspicion of other criminal activity. *Id.*; *United States v. West*, 219 F.3d 1171, 1176 (10th Cir. 2000); *Hunnicutt*, 135 F.3d at 1349. Further detention without either justification is an unreasonable seizure. *Valenzuela*, 365 F.3d at 896–97.

The Court has applied the same rule after *Rodriguez*. In *United States v. Cortez*, 965 F.3d 827, 837–38 (10th Cir. 2020), the Court examined whether the officer's conduct prolonged the stop beyond its mission and, if so, whether independent reasonable suspicion justified the delay. *See also United States v. Pettit*, 785 F.3d 1374, 1379–80 (10th Cir. 2015) (explaining that the officer must have reasonable suspicion to detain a driver beyond the time needed to complete the stop's purpose). The Court examines the objective facts known to the officer, not an after-the-fact rationale. *See United States v. Alcaraz-Arellano*, 441 F.3d 1252, 1258–59 (10th Cir. 2006).

### C. Reasonable suspicion must rest on particularized, objective facts, not a hunch.

Reasonable suspicion requires "a particularized and objective basis" for suspecting criminal activity. The government bears the burden of establishing it. An "inchoate and unparticularized suspicion or 'hunch'" is not enough. *Terry*, 392 U.S. at 27. This Circuit has repeatedly refused to sustain extended detentions that rest on innocent or ambiguous factors such as nervousness, travel on a known drug corridor, or an unusual itinerary. *See West*, 219 F.3d at 1178–79; *Hunnicutt*, 135 F.3d at 1350–51; *Valenzuela*, 365 F.3d at 897–98. Nor do such factors become suspicious simply because the officer lists them together. The officer must tie them to specific, articulable facts suggesting criminal activity. *See Santos*, 403 F.3d at 1125–26.

### D. Applied here, the extension was unlawful.

[Insert record-specific application.] The mission of the stop was complete, or reasonably should have been, when [the officer had verified the license, registration, and warrants status and could have issued the citation or warning] [ROA at __]. Rather than issue the citation and release Appellant, the officers [held him for __ minutes, pursued unrelated questioning, and awaited a canine unit] [ROA at __]. That conduct added time to the stop and was not tied to the traffic infraction. *Rodriguez*, 575 U.S. at 355–57.

The government cannot justify the delay through reasonable suspicion. The factors the officers cited, [__, __, and __], are consistent with innocent travel and do not supply a particularized basis for suspecting a crime. *West*, 219 F.3d at 1178–79; *Hunnicutt*, 135 F.3d at 1350–51. Appellant also did not consent to continued detention. Any later discovery of contraband cannot retroactively supply the missing justification. Because the prolonged detention violated the Fourth Amendment, the evidence obtained as a result must be suppressed, and the district court erred in denying the motion to suppress.
